name: NMN
lead: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a biosynthetic intermediate in the production of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), a coenzyme involved in redox reactions and a substrate for signalling enzymes such as sirtuins and PARPs [1][2]. In the body it is made from nicotinamide by the enzyme NAMPT, or from nicotinamide riboside by nicotinamide riboside kinases, and is converted to NAD+ by NMNAT enzymes [1]. It is sold as an oral supplement and, in some products, as a topical skincare ingredient [3].

People take NMN as a longevity supplement with an appearance-facing goal: the chain they describe runs from a higher NAD+ supply, to better cellular energy and repair, to more resilient tissue, skin and physical performance, and so to a younger, fitter look and more capacity to train. The starting observation is that NAD+ levels fall with age in several tissues and that restoring them improves function in rodents [2][4][5]. Human trials have generally reported that oral NMN raises blood NAD levels and is tolerated over weeks to months, with more mixed or modest results for functional outcomes; reviews state that evidence for anti-ageing effects in people is limited [6][7][8].

NMN became one of the most visible supplements in the longevity scene in the late 2010s and early 2020s, helped by the public advocacy of Harvard geneticist David Sinclair, who has described taking it daily in his book Lifespan (2019) [36]. Its regulatory status in the United States has been contested: in 2022 the FDA took the position that NMN could not be sold as a supplement because it was under investigation as a drug, and trade-press reports in September 2025 described the agency reversing course [1]. In looksmaxxing and physique communities NMN appears as an add-on in longevity and recovery supplement lists [9][10].

paras: NAD+ was first described in 1906, when Arthur Harden and William John Young found a heat-stable coferment in yeast extracts during studies of fermentation; Otto Warburg later showed in 1936 that its nicotinamide portion carries out the hydride transfer at the centre of its redox chemistry [34]. Most NAD+ in mammals is made through a salvage pathway that recycles nicotinamide, with the enzyme NAMPT producing NMN as the immediate precursor [34][12].

NMN is a nucleotide formed by attaching a phosphoribose group to nicotinamide. It is a rate-limiting intermediate in mammalian NAD+ synthesis through the NAMPT pathway [11][12]. It occurs naturally in foods such as edamame, broccoli, cabbage, cucumber and avocado at roughly 1 mg per 100 g, which Wikipedia describes as too low to supply amounts used in studies [1].

Wikipedia reports that a transporter called Slc12a8 was proposed to carry NMN into mouse intestinal cells, but this has been challenged and remains unsettled; reviews also discuss whether NMN is first converted to nicotinamide riboside outside cells before uptake [1][13]. NMN can be broken down extracellularly by the enzyme CD38, whose rising activity with age has itself been proposed as a driver of age-related NAD decline [1][14].

Sinclair and others have argued that declining NAD+ contributes to ageing and age-related disease; a review of NAD+ biology notes that human evidence on whether NAD+ falls with age is inconsistent and may depend on the tissue measured [34]. A November 2024 rat study reporting age-related NAD+ decline was withdrawn after image manipulation was found, according to Wikipedia [34].

Early biochemical work on NMN dates to the 1960s, including a 1963 report of it activating a nuclear polyadenylic acid synthesising enzyme [32]. The modern interest in NAD+ boosting grew from the discovery of sirtuins, NAD+-dependent deacetylases identified around 2000 in Leonard Guarente's laboratory, with Shin-ichiro Imai among the discoverers [34]. Imai later proposed an 'NAD World' hypothesis (2009) linking sirtuin 1 and NAMPT to mammalian ageing, which he extended as 'NAD World 2.0' in 2016 [34].

A 2011 paper from Imai's group reported that NMN treated diet- and age-induced diabetes in mice [21], and a 2016 study of long-term NMN administration in mice reported mitigation of age-associated physiological decline [5]. A 2016 paper also proposed that rising activity of the enzyme CD38 drives the age-related fall in NAD [14]. A 2018 review co-authored by Sinclair and colleagues surveyed the in vivo evidence for NAD-boosting molecules [4]. A parallel precursor, nicotinamide riboside (NR), was commercialised in the 2010s; the FDA accepted NR chloride as GRAS in 2016, and EU authorisation as a food supplement followed in 2019 and 2020 [35]. NMN is an intermediate on the NR pathway, since NR is converted to NMN before NAD+ [35].

Human work began in the 2020s. Keio University researchers reported single-dose safety in men in 2020, and the 2021 Science trial in prediabetic women and a 2021 runners' study were followed by dose-ranging and ageing trials in 2022 to 2024 [1][11][17][8][23].

NMN is promoted for skin appearance and rejuvenation, both as an oral supplement and as an ingredient in topical products; a US label for a face cream combining NMN with ectoine directs users to apply it to the face as a final skincare step and warns against use on wounds or inflamed skin [3]. No published randomised trial in the source of human studies reviewed assesses facial appearance or skin ageing as a primary outcome of NMN.
Physique-oriented forum users mention NMN alongside creatine, L-carnitine and turmeric as part of leaner-looking or endurance-oriented regimens, though such reports are anecdotal [9][15].

The appearance rationale offered by sellers and users is indirect: skin cells, muscle and connective tissue are described as depending on NAD+-dependent repair and energy metabolism, so supplying a precursor is said to support firmer skin, leaner body composition and better training capacity [2][9]. Researchers describe these as hypotheses drawn largely from cell and animal work [4][6].

NMN has no approved drug indication. It has been studied in healthy middle-aged and older adults, prediabetes, exercise performance, sleep, vascular stiffness and, in registered trials, immune ageing, ovarian reserve and polycystic ovary syndrome [8][11][16][17][18][19][20].

Supplemental NMN is proposed to raise NAD+ levels, which in turn supports sirtuin and mitochondrial function [2][13]. In mouse studies, NMN improved glucose handling in diet- and age-induced diabetes and long-term administration mitigated age-associated physiological decline [21][5]. Reviews caution that NAD+ metabolism is complex, that animal findings do not always transfer to humans, and that factors affecting the success or risks of NAD+ supplementation remain poorly understood [22][4].

A 2023 review of human clinical trials of NMN concluded that it appears safe over the periods studied and raises NAD+ status, while noting that most evidence for anti-ageing effects comes from cell and animal work and that human trials are few and short [6]. A 2022 review similarly discussed promise and safety concerns [7].

A multicentre randomised, placebo-controlled trial in 80 healthy middle-aged adults tested several oral doses for 60 days, reporting effects on NAD levels, walking and other measures of health [8]. A 10-week randomised trial in postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were overweight or obese found that NMN increased insulin-stimulated muscle insulin signalling and sensitivity, as reported in Science [11]. A trial in older adults reported higher blood NAD levels, maintained walking speed and improved sleep quality [23], while a 12-week trial in older Japanese adults assessed sleep, fatigue and physical performance [24]. A randomised study in amateur runners reported enhanced aerobic capacity [17], and a randomised trial examined arterial stiffness after long-term NMN [16]. Some of these trials were funded or supported by supplement manufacturers.

Registered trials include studies in diminished ovarian reserve, repeated IVF failure, polycystic ovary syndrome, immunosenescence in metabolic disease, frailty and exercise tolerance in older adults, and a safety study in a rare congenital disorder of glycosylation [19][25][20][18][26][27].

Short-term human trials have reported good tolerability, and a Keio University single-dose study found doses of up to 500 mg safe in men, according to Wikipedia [6][1]. Mild gastrointestinal effects and flushing have been reported with NAD+ precursors in general [28]. Long-term safety in humans is not established, and reviews raise theoretical questions about boosting NAD+ in people with existing cancers or other conditions, which remain unresolved [22][7]. Product quality and composition vary between suppliers [7].

Supplement companies have marketed NMN heavily with anti-ageing claims, which Wikipedia notes are not proven in humans [1]. Sinclair, a Harvard professor and author of Lifespan (September 2019, co-written with Matthew LaPlante), has said he takes NMN and resveratrol daily and discusses his routine on social media and in the book; in 2023 he co-founded the supplement company Tally Health [36]. Critical coverage includes a 2015 Scientific American blog post by Stipp titled 'Beyond Resveratrol: The Anti-Aging NAD Fad' [1].

Sinclair's work has also drawn disputes. Wikipedia reports that a 2005 paper concluded resveratrol was not a direct SIR2 activator, that GSK shut down his former company Sirtris's resveratrol programme, and that in 2024 other longevity researchers criticised a claim about a supplement reversing ageing in dogs [36]. Supporters of NAD+ research point instead to the independent trials listed above [8][11].

According to Wikipedia, in 2022 the FDA took the position that NMN could not be marketed as a dietary supplement because it was being investigated as a pharmaceutical drug [1]. Wikipedia's article on David Sinclair states that Metro Biotech, a company he co-founded in 2015 to develop NAD+ precursors, had registered NMN in investigational new drug applications and urged the FDA to remove NMN from the supplement market [36]. Amazon reportedly removed NMN supplements in early 2023, citing FDA actions [1].

On 30 September 2025 the trade publication NutraIngredients reported that the FDA had declared NMN lawful in dietary supplements, and Wikipedia cites a December 2025 FDA letter concerning a notification for beta-NMN [1]. Legal status elsewhere varies by jurisdiction and product form, and supplement quality differs between suppliers [7].

subs.h: Use in physique and longevity communities
paras: On T Nation, users report adding NMN to creatine and electrolyte drinks, listing it among daily supplements next to ubiquinol and taurine, and asking whether it can rejuvenate arteries for ageing lifters or heal intestinal damage [15][10][29][30]. A user on testosterone therapy who had begun both resveratrol and NMN reported a spike in estradiol and wondered about a connection; no study cited here examines that [31].

lore.intro: NMN is discussed in training forums as a longevity and recovery add-on, usually alongside creatine, CoQ10 or resveratrol [15][10][31].

claims.claim: NMN restores NAD+ and slows or reverses ageing
claims.believers: Proponents argue that NAD+ declines with age and that topping it up rejuvenates tissues, and forum users describe taking it for joints, circulation and looking leaner [9][29].
claims.experts: Rodent studies show benefits, while human trials show raised NAD levels with modest or mixed functional results, and reviews state that anti-ageing effects in people are not established [5][6][7].

claims.believers: A T Nation user cited a video claiming NMN rejuvenates arteries and veins and asked other older lifters whether they take it [29].
claims.experts: A randomised trial examined arterial stiffness after long-term supplementation, and mouse work links NAD+ and vascular ageing, but no definitive human result is established [16][33].

claims.claim: NMN could heal intestinal damage in inflammatory bowel disease
claims.believers: A forum user asked whether it could heal intestinal damage in a thread about steroid cycles with IBD [30].
claims.experts: No published human trial cited here has tested NMN for inflammatory bowel disease.

claims.believers: Some users report running feeling better and adding NMN to training drinks [9][15].
claims.experts: One randomised study in amateur runners reported improved aerobic capacity and another in older adults reported maintained walking speed, but trials are small and short [17][23].

claims.claim: NMN works like a sirtuin-activating anti-ageing pill, building on resveratrol
claims.believers: Sinclair has said he takes NMN and resveratrol daily because he says they activate SIRT1, and followers repeat that routine [36].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that a 2005 study concluded resveratrol was not a SIR2 activator, and reviews say NAD+ metabolism is complex and human anti-ageing benefit is not established [36][22][7].

claims.claim: NMN is better than nicotinamide riboside, or vice versa
claims.believers: Brand communities argue over which precursor is more efficient, citing transporter findings in mice or the commercial track record of NR [35].
claims.experts: Reviews note NR is converted to NMN and that whether NMN enters cells directly via Slc12a8 is unsettled, so comparisons remain open [1][13][35].

claims.claim: The FDA ban on NMN was commercially motivated
claims.believers: Some users and industry voices point to Metro Biotech's drug filings as evidence the 2022 position favoured a competitor [36].
claims.experts: Wikipedia states the FDA's stated reason was that NMN was under drug investigation, and that the position was later reversed for beta-NMN [1][36].
